items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a lone porter trudging the mountain trail every morning, hauling a crate up switchback after switchback. Rain, snow, aching knees — never late, never off. That relentless, unglamorous grind is the whole meaning: <kanji>diligence</kanji>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the school field, beside one bare <radical>tree</radical>, a lone performer balances six spinning plates arranged in a <radical>cross</radical>, one on each finger. items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 張 as one enormous <radical>bow</radical> spanning the mountain trail, its string humming <radical>long</radical> behind the vending machine. Hikers count each bow strung this tight before trusting it to hold their weight across the gap. That count is the whole job of this character: the <kanji>counter for bows and stringed instruments</kanji>, pulled drum-tight.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the trail, the hiker everyone calls <reading>Chow</reading> counts the taut bows by the vending machine. He taps each string and grunts <reading>ちょう</reading> under his breath — one, two, three.
items.description: As a counter, this kanji counts things held taut by a string, such as bows and stringed instruments, not flat sheets or long thin objects, which take other counters. The verb sense stretch or spread is the same idea: pulling something tight, which is why the same character became the counting word for anything strung that way.

He waves; the water waves back late — exactly what it means to <kanji>reflect</kanji>.

items.description: This kanji covers more than sorry: the same character also carries formal thanks and, in some compounds, an outright refusal or decline. Underneath all three is one idea, a formal spoken response rather than plain regret, so context decides whether it reads as apology, gratitude, or a firm no.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail narrows to a knife-edge ridge, pinching to nothing between two sheer drops. A lone <radical>person</radical> stands there shouting into a <radical>mouth</radical>-shaped gap in the rock. The echo bounces toward a tiny <radical>village</radical> clinging to the far cliff. No one has ever reached that village and no one ever will — the position is <kanji>precipitous</kanji>, impregnable, sealed off from the world.
items.reading_mnemonic: Guarding that narrow ledge is <reading>Ken</reading>, the shiba who never leaves his wall of antique swords. Every hiker who nears the edge gets one warning bark of <reading>けん</reading> before he bares a blade in his teeth.
items.description: Beyond the literal steep-cliff picture, this kanji usually carries a broader sense of danger or risk in real vocabulary — insurance, adventure, hazard — rather than physical steepness itself.

example_sentences.japanese: 夜、この道を歩くのは危険です。
example_sentences.english: Walking this road at night is dangerous.
example_sentences.furigana: 夜[よる]、この道[みち]を歩[ある]くのは危[き]険[けん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は保険の仕事をしています。
example_sentences.english: He works in insurance.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は保[ほ]険[けん]の仕[し]事[ごと]をしています。

example_sentences.japanese: 車の保険はとても高いです。
example_sentences.english: Car insurance is very expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: 車[くるま]の保[ほ]険[けん]はとても高[たか]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 輸 as one strange <radical>vehicle</radical>: a wagon's wheels bolted onto a hollowed boat hull. A lone <radical>person</radical> poles it, standing on one plank of bare <radical>ground</radical>. A curved <radical>sword</radical> in his belt scrapes the hull into a <radical>moon</radical>-shaped curve. Crates get loaded on and it shoves off. Wheels spin uselessly underwater, the hull scrapes stone on land, yet the ugly thing drags everything across. That is <kanji>transport</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The ferryman poling this contraption never learns anyone's name, so he calls every passenger the same drawn-out word as the wheels hit water: a long <reading>you</reading>. That same stretched syllable is the reading <reading>ゆ</reading>, hollered once as the crates lurch forward and the hull scrapes off from the bank.

example_sentences.japanese: この工場は魚を外国に輸出しています。
example_sentences.english: This factory exports fish to foreign countries.
example_sentences.furigana: この工[こう]場[じょう]は魚[さかな]を外[がい]国[こく]に輸[ゆ]出[しゅつ]しています。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは肉をたくさん輸入しています。
example_sentences.english: We import a lot of meat.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは肉[にく]をたくさん輸[ゆ]入[にゅう]しています。

example_sentences.japanese: その会社は野菜も輸出しています。
example_sentences.english: That company also exports vegetables.
example_sentences.furigana: その会[かい]社[しゃ]は野[や]菜[さい]も輸[ゆ]出[しゅつ]しています。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer plants one <radical>hand</radical> flat on the last onigiri, elbow cocked out like a <radical>halberd</radical> guarding it. He shoots the whole line a <radical>barb</radical>ed glare. He mutters that the shelf, the till, and the entire store were built for him. Nobody else gets within an arm's length of it. That elbows-out glare is pure <kanji>ego</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The staff have nicknamed him <reading>Gah</reading>. Every time a hand drifts toward his onigiri, he barks <reading>が</reading> without even looking up, elbows still locked around the shelf.
items.description: As a stand-alone word, 我 (われ) is formal and literary — it isn't how someone says "I" in an ordinary conversation. Day to day it survives mostly inside set compounds about endurance and self rather than standing alone.

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は公園で怪我しました。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother got injured at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は公[こう]園[えん]で怪[け]我[が]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 足の怪我はもう大丈夫ですか。
example_sentences.english: Is your leg injury already all right?
example_sentences.furigana: 足[あし]の怪[け]我[が]はもう大[だい]丈[じょう]夫[ぶ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 頭を怪我して、病院に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I hurt my head and went to the hospital.
example_sentences.furigana: 頭[あたま]を怪[け]我[が]して、病[びょう]院[いん]に行[い]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> on the left; on the right <radical>two</radical> bars over <radical>ground</radical>, each on a <radical>stick</radical>, <radical>split</radical> into legs at the foot. A tray, lifted with both hands for somebody above to take: to <kanji>submit</kanji> a thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kyou is the offering-bearer who never lowers the tray. He walks the entire length of the hall with it over his head, announcing himself at every pillar — 「<reading>きょう</reading>」 — until somebody finally takes the weight off him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 降 as a steep staircase cut into a mountainside, above a distant <radical>village</radical> at the bottom, two hurried <radical>trailing foot</radical>prints stamped down the steps. A crate tips off the vending machine and thunders down every step, bottles bouncing all the way down. A hill with feet already halfway down it: <kanji>descend</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi treks up that same trail himself to restock the vending machine. When the last case slips from his arms and crashes down every step behind him, he just sighs 「<reading>こう</reading>」 — more <reading>cough</reading> than word — and watches it disappear downhill.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅でバスを降ります。
example_sentences.english: I get off the bus at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]でバスを降[お]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝から雨が降っています。
example_sentences.english: It has been raining since this morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]から雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 冬は雪がたくさん降ります。
example_sentences.english: It snows a lot in winter.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]は雪[ゆき]がたくさん降[お]ります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 婦 as a <radical>woman</radical> named Fumi, sweeping Grandma Kane's shrine steps at dawn under the <radical>cover</radical> of a long apron of <radical>cloth</radical>. Her <radical>broom</radical> scrapes stone in the same rhythm every morning while the shrine cats scatter. She works top to bottom without looking up: the picture of a <kanji>lady</kanji> running her own household.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine gate, Fumi leans her broom against the rail and blows out a long <reading>phew</reading> — a breathy 「<reading>ふ</reading>」 that scatters the incense smoke. Then she picks the broom up to finish the steps.

example_sentences.japanese: あの夫婦はいつも公園を歩いています。
example_sentences.english: That married couple always walks in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: あの夫[ふう]婦[ふ]はいつも公[こう]園[えん]を歩[ある]いています。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の母は主婦です。
example_sentences.english: My mother is a housewife.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の母[はは]は主[しゅ]婦[ふ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: その夫婦は来月新しい家に住みます。
example_sentences.english: That couple will live in a new house next month.
example_sentences.furigana: その夫[ふう]婦[ふ]は来[らい]月[げつ]新[あたら]しい家[いえ]に住[す]みます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> at the bottom, above her a <radical>broom</radical> on its <radical>stick</radical>, <radical>ground</radical> ruled across top. Not sweeping somebody's house — the broom, floor, roof are hers: the <kanji>wife</kanji> running them.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sai is the one who actually decides. Ask her husband anything and he glances sideways at her first; she gives one flat 「<reading>さい</reading>」 and that is the answer on behalf of both of them. さい settles it.
